forces: Soprano solo, mixed chorus and orchestra with organ
performers: Lisa della Casa, soprano; Wiener Staatsopernchor; Wiener Philharmoniker; Franz Sauer, organ; Bruno Walter, conductor
recorded: 26 July 1956, Small Festival Hall, Salzburg; live
intro: Lisa della Casa’s soprano brings back the Introitus psalm melody, now asking for eternal light. The choir closes the Requiem with the earlier Kyrie fugue, its racing lines finally stripped down to a bare D and A.

sections.label: A · The soprano asks for light
sections.mNote: The Introitus psalm melody carries the Communion words

sections.label: B · The choir remembers the opening
sections.mNote: Choral phrases from the Introitus return in order

sections.label: C · The Kyrie fugue returns
sections.mNote: Two interlocking themes now carry cum sanctis tuis

sections.label: Coda · Adagio, then a bare fifth
sections.mNote: The running voices settle on D and A

cues.title: Light from one voice
cues.text: A short wind phrase opens onto the soprano’s prayer for eternal light. Her melody comes from the Introitus psalm verse, in B♭ major. The strings keep their quick figures moving beneath her longer notes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 95, compared with the Introitus on pp. 3–4. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/79/IMSLP758680-PMLP2751-Mozart_Requiem%2C_K.626_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The choir joins the prayer
cues.text: Tenors and basses take up the prayer, followed by altos and sopranos. The strings continue their quick figures through the handover. Basset horns and bassoons return alongside the growing choir.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 95, bars 59–60: lower choral entries, followed by alto and soprano, with returning woodwinds.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The old words return
cues.text: The Communion prayer makes room for the old words, “Requiem aeternam”. The returning Introitus combines its long opening theme with quicker phrases on “Dona eis”; these move from altos to sopranos, then through the lower voices.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, pp. 96–98: the later Introitus music returns with Requiem aeternam and dona eis requiem.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Süssmayr explains the return
cues.text: In his letter to the publishers Breitkopf & Härtel on 8 February 1800, Süssmayr explains his completion: he repeats the Kyrie fugue “in order to give the work more unity”.
cues.evidence: Süssmayr to Breitkopf & Härtel, 8 February 1800, quoted in Leopold Nowak’s Neue Mozart-Ausgabe foreword, Requiem, volume 2, pp. XIV–XV; wording from the English translation. https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/pdf/nma_14_-23_-3_eng.pdf

cues.title: Two themes run together
cues.text: The Kyrie fugue returns at Allegro, now carrying “Cum sanctis tuis” — with your saints. One theme strides in longer notes; the other runs in semiquavers. Basses begin the first, altos the second, and the two keep finding new partners throughout the choir.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, pp. 98–99: Allegro, bass subject and the quicker alto entry. The Latin is the Communion prayer.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Salzburg, July 1956
cues.text: On 26 July 1956, Bruno Walter conducts the Requiem in Salzburg’s Small Festival Hall. Lisa della Casa sings the soprano part and Franz Sauer plays the organ. The same concert includes Mozart’s G-minor Symphony No. 25.
cues.evidence: Vienna Philharmonic concert archive, listing date, venue, conductor, soloists, organist and programme: https://www.wienerphilharmoniker.at/en/konzerte/salzburg-festival/512/

cues.title: Only D and A
cues.text: The fugue ends with a sudden broadening to Adagio. The running voices come together on the last words, “Quia pius es” — for you are merciful. The final chord contains only D and A: all that crowded singing ends on a bare fifth.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 104: Adagio, final Communion words and the open D–A fifth. This note concerns the musical close before the recording’s remaining concert sound.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The lower voices take over
transitions.from: A · The soprano asks for light
transitions.to: B · The choir remembers the opening
transitions.how: As the B♭-major soprano passage ends, tenors and basses begin the choral prayer. Altos follow, then sopranos. Basset horns and bassoons return forte, while the strings carry their quick figures straight through the handover. The bass line becomes busy again beneath the overlapping voices.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 95, bars 57–60: the end of the solo, choral entries and returning woodwinds.

transitions.title: A major releases the fugue
transitions.from: B · The choir remembers the opening
transitions.how: The choir holds an A-major chord under a fermata, the bass resting on A. Then Allegro: the choral basses and bassoons begin the Kyrie’s D-minor subject. Altos enter with its running companion, doubled by second violins and basset horns. The old fugue carries the Communion words.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 98, bars 80–84: held dominant and the first two fugal entries.

transitions.title: The voices stop running
transitions.to: Coda · Adagio, then a bare fifth
transitions.how: The last semiquaver runs reach a halt, and Adagio brings all four choral parts together. A fermata suspends the phrase before “Quia pius es”. The bass descends towards D; the final chord leaves D and A alone, with no third between them.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 104, bars 130–133: the final Adagio, fermata and open fifth.

source.title: Mozart–Süssmayr Requiem, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover unabridged reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 95–104: the Introitus psalm music returns for soprano and choir, followed by the Kyrie fugue with Communion words and the final Adagio.

timeline.note: Basset horns, bassoons and strings recall the short wind link before the Introitus psalm.
The soprano sings Lux aeterna over quick violin and cello figures.
Lower choral voices begin the response, then altos and sopranos join; the quick string figures continue.
The later Introitus prayer returns with its overlapping vocal lines and trumpet and timpani accents.
The choir softens towards a held A-major chord, with the strings and bass settling beneath it.
Basses begin the Kyrie subject; altos answer with the running theme, doubled by basset horns and second violins.
The fugue’s two themes pass through all four choral parts, with the strings doubling their lines.
At Adagio the voices come together; the closing chord contains only D and A.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Lisa della Casa (soprano), Wiener Staatsopernchor (chorus), Wiener Philharmoniker (orchestra), Franz Sauer (organ), Bruno Walter (conductor)
fields.note: Lisa della Casa is the soprano soloist for this movement. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Traditional Süssmayr Communio, adapting Mozart’s Introitus and Kyrie; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified.
fields.note: The NMA labels the movement Süssmayr after Mozart’s Introitus and Kyrie. This is not an independently completed final movement in Mozart’s surviving manuscript. Süssmayr’s 1800 letter explains reuse of the Kyrie fugue; Constanze’s reported instruction from Mozart is testimony, not independent verification of a complete plan. File duration includes a retained live-recording tail after the estimated musical close.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The primary concert archive identifies Thursday 26 July 1956; Commons, Internet Archive and the discography agree. This is the live performance date, not the date of first publication, a later commercial issue, digitisation or upload.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Small Festival Hall (Kleines Festspielhaus), Salzburg, Austria
fields.note: The Vienna Philharmonic event archive supplies Small Festival Hall. Internet Archive calls the source a live Salzburg Festival performance; the discography uses the broader Festspielhaus designation. No studio session, microphone layout or original recording medium is inferred.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The carrier actually used for this upload is unidentified. The discography lists Cetra, Nuova Era, Seven Seas and Orfeo issues of this performance. Session medium, tape generation, speed correction, equalisation, noise reduction, editing and restoration settings remain unknown; no such processing is inferred from the transfer’s sound.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying Mozart–Süssmayr composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Mozart died in 1791 and Süssmayr in 1803; the traditional full score was published in 1800. This is a term-based assessment of the historical composition, not a worldwide clearance, a licence for a modern critical edition, or evidence about the sound recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — territorial recording claim: Commons applies PD-EU-audio; upstream Internet Archive applies Public Domain Mark 1.0.
fields.note: The documented fact is the sources’ sound-recording rights assertion. PD-EU-audio is territorial: US status is not established, and no worldwide clearance is claimed. Public Domain Mark is not CC0 or a performer’s licence. The 1956 performance date does not prove first lawful publication or communication before 1963; that history is unestablished. The known 1996 Orfeo issue and 2018 uploads are not substituted for it. Admission therefore uses the explicit Commons PD-EU-audio route, not a calculated pre-1963-publication claim.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
